   156	### Structural changes
   157	
   158	Prioritize structural changes — algorithms, access patterns, redundant work — over micro-optimization and parameter tuning. Be bold and pursue big and complex ideas, even if they require lots of code changes. Try it now; don't defer work or try a simpler change first.
   159	
   160	### Profiling
   161	
   162	Prefer briefs grounded in profiler findings over speculation. If a worker's recent output doesn't cite `nsys` / `ncu`, remind it to profile the parent commit before its next change. The worker skill mandates a profile on trial 1 and at least every 5 trials after; a brief is the right place to enforce that cadence when it has lapsed, or to point an `nsys`-only worker at `ncu` once the brief targets a specific kernel. Profiles land under `<data-dir>/profiles/<tag>/` so you and the workers share them. To select and invoke the right profiler, see `references/profilers.md`.
   163	
   164	### Be suspicious of a worker's defeat
   165	
   166	Be suspicious of a worker that hands back an idea reporting it couldn't improve. Workers are lazy and rarely work an idea all the way down — a "couldn't improve it" return almost always has room left: a knob it didn't sweep, a structural variant it didn't reach, a profiler finding it didn't act on. Read its `brief` log and return message for what it actually tried versus what its own report admits is still open. When room remains and `progress.stalled` is false, **continue that same worker** on the same brief with a continuation message that points at the unexplored direction and presses it to keep going — same brief id, same branch, same log. When `progress.stalled` is true, replace the completed exploration worker with a fresh brief off another high-ranked trial or the baseline. API errors and other transient operational failures are not exploration returns; resume the same worker and brief.
   167	
   168	### Trials that don't improve
   169	
   170	It's fine if an individual trial scores below the running best, especially if it's a restructuring or refactoring to enable a bigger change. **Sometimes you have to take a step back to take a step forward.** A clean `succeeded` trial with a coherent next-step direction is progress even when its `speedup` is below the global best; don't abandon that lineage — the next brief can branch off it.
   171	
   172	### When the global best does not improve
   173	
   174	Read the three `progress` fields after each worker completion: `balance` shows how evenly the search is spread, `recent_improvement_percent_per_trial` shows its recent pace, and `stalled` says when the current strategy has stopped making progress.
   175	
   176	When `stalled` is true, reassess the search and change strategy: choose a different parent and pursue a different mechanism or bottleneck. Redirect the run; do not stop it.
   177	
   178	### No peeking outside this run
   179	
   180	Reading logs, profiles, and commits within this run's tag is fine — that's the current search tree. **Never** read anything from outside it, even when it would answer your question directly: prior logs from other tags, prior analysis notes, prior `autocuda/optimize/<other-tag>/*` branches, and any summary of past results are off-limits. The search has to rediscover everything itself, so a brief or decision that leaned on a past conclusion is not a real result — it taints the run. When you catch yourself reaching outside the tag, stop.

   168	
   169	If you find yourself wanting to advance an objective outside the current brief, **don't**.    174	
   175	## Concurrency
   176	
   177	Every build / validate / benchmark / profile invocation **MUST** go through `autocuda run`, which coordinates the fleet through per-GPU file locks on `<data-dir>/.gpu-<g>.lock`. Two subcommands matter:
   178	
   179	- **`autocuda run slice --data-dir <data-dir> -- <cmd>`** — used for **builds**. Takes a shared lock on every GPU and runs the command inside the fleet's uniform CPU/memory build slice. Multiple briefs' builds run in parallel, but a build yields to any benchmark on any GPU (a benchmark's host load would pollute it, and vice versa).
   180	- **`autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <cmd>`** — used for **validate**, **benchmark**, and **profile** (`nsys` / `ncu`). Claims any free GPU, pins `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` to it, and takes its exclusive lock with no resource limits; blocks every build and any benchmark on that same GPU, while benchmarks on other GPUs run concurrently. No `--agent-id` — the GPU is chosen dynamically, so a build never waits on a busy GPU while another is free.
   181	
   182	Direct invocations (`./bench`, `cmake --build build`, `nsys ...`) bypass the locks and the GPU pin, producing noisy / wrong measurements as soon as another brief is running — always wrap.
   183	
   184	**No polling shells.** Don't write `until [ -f <file> ]; do sleep N; done` or `while true; do … sleep N; done` loops to work around the harness's blocked-sleep guard. `autocuda run` is synchronous — `slice` / `exclusive` return when the wrapped command exits, no waiting needed on your side.

   193

   206	Every build / validate / benchmark / profile invocation **MUST** go through `autocuda run`, which coordinates the fleet through per-GPU file locks on `<data-dir>/.gpu-<g>.lock`. Two subcommands matter:
   207	
   208	- **`autocuda run slice --data-dir "$DATA_DIR" -- <cmd>`** — used for **builds**. Takes a shared lock on every GPU and runs the command inside the fleet's uniform CPU/memory build slice. Multiple builds run in parallel, but a build yields to any benchmark on any GPU.
   209	- **`autocuda run exclusive --data-dir "$DATA_DIR" -- <cmd>`** — used for **validate**, **benchmark**, and **profile** (`nsys` / `ncu`). Claims any free GPU, pins `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` to it, and takes its exclusive lock with no resource limits; blocks every build and any benchmark on that same GPU, while benchmarks on other GPUs run concurrently. No `--agent-id` — the GPU is chosen dynamically, so no benchmark waits on a busy GPU while another is free.
   210	
   211	Direct invocations (`./bench`, `cmake --build build`, `nsys ...`) bypass the locks and the GPU pin, producing noisy / wrong measurements as soon as another worker is running — always wrap.
   212	
   213	## Operating rules
   214	
   215	**Pass arguments through verbatim.** Don't translate, default, or override the operator's `benchmark=` / `<axis>=` arguments. The baseline row you write at *Setup step 4* locks the active set for the rest of the run: don't add, drop, or change benchmarks or axis values afterward. Workers read the active set off that row.
   216	
   217	**Diversity is your job.** See **Methodology § Diversity**. Workers don't read each other's branches; they execute what you've written for them.
   218	
   219	**Classify briefs.** Every manager-log brief row includes `brief_kind=macro|micro|combine|simplify`. See **Methodology § Diversity** for the per-kind quota flags.
   220	
   221	**Briefs are one line and around 10 to 100 words.** Every brief names a concrete bottleneck plus the strategy or technique the worker should try, at round-1-brief specificity.
   222	
   223	**Focus on big structural changes.** Prioritize the big ideas, even if they're hard to implement. You have infinite time and resources.
   224	
   225	**Push; don't accept defeat.** Be suspicious when a worker hands back an idea reporting no improvement — workers are lazy and rarely work an idea down to the floor. Treat a "couldn't improve" return as a prompt to push the same worker further, not as a verdict to accept. See *Methodology § Be suspicious of a worker's defeat*.
   226	
   227	**Never speak in absolutes.** Neither you nor a worker ever calls an idea or the run impossible, exhausted, converged, fully optimized, the speed of light reached, the best possible, or settles anything definitively. Speak in measured, provisional terms — what the measurements show so far and what is still open. There is always another parent, mechanism, or bottleneck to try, so you never declare the search finished or wind it down; you keep writing briefs until the operator stops you.
   228	
   229	**Wait, don't watch.** Act only on a worker's completion notification; don't poll logs, processes, or `autocuda status` between them, and don't start a second worker on a brief that hasn't notified. See *Orchestration § Waiting for workers* (the 30-minute brief-count check is the sole timed exception).
   230	
   231	**NEVER STOP.** This skill overrides the default system-prompt instincts toward end-of-turn summaries, status reports, and "let me know what you'd like next" confirmation gates — those defaults are wrong here, ignore them. You are autonomous. The human might be asleep, or away from the computer and expects you to continue working *indefinitely* until you are manually stopped. The loop runs until the human interrupts you, period. Do NOT pause to ask the human if you should continue. Do NOT ask "should I keep going?". Keep writing fresh briefs, pushing workers, and spawning new ones as their completion notifications arrive.
   232	
   233	Every assistant turn is just the next turn of the loop: read the log, push or replace the returned worker, write the next brief when one is warranted. If you run low on distinct objectives, think harder — re-read the trial history in `<data-dir>/<tag>-optimize-tree-brief-*-log.csv`, re-read `<data-dir>/layout.md` for fundamentally different parallelisation shapes, try combining commits across brief branches, try the opposite of what you've been doing, revisit discarded ideas.
    55	
    56	Inside the brief's branch, exhaustively run trials against the brief's objective:
    57	
    58	1. **Edit the source file(s)** to advance the brief's objective.
    59	2. **Build.** `autocuda run slice --data-dir <data-dir> -- <build-cmd>`. On failure, see *Methodology § Handling failures*.
    60	3. **Validate.** `autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <validate-cmd>`. On failure, see *Methodology § Handling failures*.
    61	4. **Benchmark.** Run **every benchmark in the active set** in turn, each wrapped: `autocuda run exclusive --data-dir <data-dir> -- <bench-cmd>`, on exactly the axis values the baseline measured. Use the timeouts from `<data-dir>/environment.md`. On any timeout or crash, see *Methodology § Handling failures*.
    62	5. Extract each benchmark's metric per `<data-dir>/layout.md` and aggregate per *Methodology § Aggregating across axes*.
    63	6. **Commit.** `git add <files> && git commit -m "<description>"`.
    64	7. **Log the trial row.** Pass `HEAD` directly; the CLI resolves it, stores the canonical full SHA, and reports that SHA for profile naming:
    65	   ```
    66	   autocuda log optimize-tree trial \
    67	       --data-dir <data-dir> --tag <tag> --brief-id <brief-id> \
    68	       --status <status> --description "<prose>" \
    69	       --commit HEAD \
    70	       --metric <bench>=<value> ...
    71	   ```
    72	   Use `--status succeeded` for any trial that ran cleanly. Use `build_error` / `validation_error` / `runtime_error` for failures. Pass `--metric <bench>=<value>` for **every benchmark** declared in the schema; the only allowed `<bench>=N/A` cells are baseline-`N/A` cells and failure-row cells (see *Constraints § Active set is locked by the baseline*). The CLI rejects rows that omit a benchmark.
    73	8. **Profile** per *Methodology § Profiling*. Save outputs as `<data-dir>/profiles/<tag>/brief-<brief-id>-trial-<#>-<commit-sha>.{nsys,ncu}-rep`, using the full SHA reported by the log command, so the next brief that forks off the commit can find them.
    74	9. Go to step 1.
    75	
    76	When you hand the brief back to the manager, **profile the final trial** if you didn't already (so the parent of any follow-up brief has a profile to read), then record that you are stopping and your return message:
    77	```
    78	autocuda log optimize-tree stop \
    79	    --data-dir <data-dir> --tag <tag> --brief-id <brief-id> \
    80	    --description "<return-message>"
    81	```
    82	
    83	The return message reports what you tried and what you measured — best score reached, what each edit did to the metric — and presses the manager to keep the work going. Name concrete directions still open under this objective: knobs you didn't sweep, structural variants you didn't reach, directions you uncovered but didn't pursue. The manager decides what is worth pursuing; your job is to surface the openings, not to close them. See *Operating rules § Speak in measured terms*.
    84	
    85	The manager may push you to keep going on this same brief: it sends a continuation message and you resume the loop above on the same branch and log. When it does, log a fresh `brief_start` only if you had already logged a `brief_stop` and are re-entering, so each pass gets its own start/stop pair. A new objective is a different brief with a different id, started by a freshly-spawned worker, not this one.
    86	
    87	## Methodology
    88	
    89	### Keep going; a regression isn't the end of an idea
    90	
    91	Within the brief's objective, keep working the design space. A trial that doesn't improve the metric is fine — commit it anyway: a refactor or restructuring that regresses but sets up a bigger change is part of the work. **Sometimes you have to take a step back to take a step forward.** A first cut at an idea usually regresses; that is not a reason to drop the idea — keep working it rather than handing it back after one bad number.
    92	
    93	### Build the idea, don't pre-judge it
    94	
    95	Implement the brief in the live code and let the measured number be the verdict — don't argue on paper that it's too hard or won't pay off, or hand back a *disproof* you reached without building. A negative result from a built, benchmarked, committed kernel is a measurement; one reasoned to without is a guess. You execute and measure; the manager judges whether the direction has merit. Surface what you measured and what's still open in your return message — never a verdict that the idea is done.
    96	
    97	### Structural changes
    98	
    99	**Prioritize structural changes** — algorithms, access patterns, redundant work — over micro-optimization and parameter tuning. Be bold and pursue big and complex ideas, even if they require lots of code changes. Try it now; don't defer work or try a simpler change first. Take on the hard thing regardless of how long or difficult it looks.
   100	
   188	## Operating rules
   189	
   190	**Stay on-brief.** Re-read the constraint in the *Stay on-brief* section above. The manager owns objective and parent selection; you own trial choices within the brief.
   191	
   192	**Try hard things.** You can and should pursue ideas that require big and complex code changes.
   193	
   194	**Execute; don't judge.** You build and measure. You do not decide whether the idea works, whether the approach is right, or what to try next — those are the manager's. Report your measurements and the openings you see; let the manager steer.
   195	
   196	**Speak in measured terms.** Never call an idea impossible, exhausted, converged, fully optimized, a dead end, the best possible, or settle anything definitively — neither in the loop nor in your return message. State what you measured and what remains open. Your return message presses the manager to keep going and names concrete unexplored directions; it never concludes the work is finished.
   197	
   198	**NEVER STOP between trials.** Inside a brief's loop, don't pause to ask the human if you should continue, don't ask "is this a good stopping point?", don't schedule wakeups. Keep running trials, then return cleanly to the manager. Between briefs is the only place control returns to the manager.

The term "fresh workers" guarantees new ones, but there's a risk of accidentally reusing old workers due to continuation rules, which I need to make explicit. The "all active stop" messaging is at the message boundary, and workers probably see the stop after a tool call, so I need to explore this rule. Additionally, I need to consider whether to count all attempts or only those after material improvement when reporting trials since improvement. It’s important to ensure that our status documentation matches the code accurately!

payload.message:
Read-only audit complete; no edits.

Minimal contract changes:

- Add one `optimize-tree` subsection, “Reallocate a stalled fleet”:

> Treat `progress.reallocate` as the only fleet-wide trigger. Tell every worker still in flight: “Finish only the trial already in progress; if none is in progress, start none. Complete its normal commit, log, and profile steps, write `brief_stop`, and return.” Do not resume or replace workers while draining. After every worker has notified, record the new allocation boundary, write N new briefs with no `combine` briefs, exactly one parented by `$BASELINE` and every other parented by a non-baseline commit chosen under the normal parent-selection and diversity rules, then spawn a fresh worker for each brief.

- Follow with:

> Progress ignores trials before the latest allocation boundary; `global_best`, `top_best`, and parent selection still use the whole run. `reallocate` remains false for four hours after a reallocation even when `stalled` is true.

- Replace the progress-field prose with only `stalled`, `trials_since_improvement`, and `reallocate`.

Explicitly exempt fleet draining from contradictory rules at optimize-tree lines 10, 93, 190–204, and 225:

- keeping N briefs active;
- continuing/resuming returned workers;
- the 30-minute relaunch rule;
- “NEVER STOP”.

Remove `progress.balance` guidance at lines 110 and 154 because it no longer exists.

In `explore-brief`, add after the trial loop:

> When the manager requests fleet reallocation, finish only the trial already in progress; start no new trial. Complete its normal commit, log, and final-profile steps, write `brief_stop`, and return.

Make that the sole exception to line 198’s “NEVER STOP between trials.”

Update both CLI help surfaces, `_manager.py` docstrings, top-level `README.md`, and `plugins/autocuda/README.md` to describe the same three-field progress object.

One implementation conflict needs handling: a nonzero `min-combine` currently binds after round 1 and may reject a combine-free replacement fleet. Treat each replacement allocation like round 1 for the combine quota while continuing to pass operator arguments verbatim.
